entry: Biological defense response of body tissues to harmful stimuli. Triggers include physical trauma, [[Pathogen|pathogens]], irritants, toxins, overuse, autoimmunity, allergens and foreign bodies. The five cardinal signs of acute inflammation are heat, pain, redness, swelling and loss of function (Latin *calor*, *dolor*, *rubor*, *tumor* and *functio laesa*). It is a generic response and is considered a mechanism of [[Immune system|innate immunity]]. Its function is to eliminate the initial cause of cell injury, clear damaged cells and tissues, and initiate repair. Acute inflammation is a short-term process that usually appears within minutes or hours and ceases when the injurious stimulus is removed. Chronic inflammation is prolonged and involves simultaneous destruction and healing of tissue. Too much chronic inflammation is associated with diseases such as hay fever, periodontal disease, [[Atherosclerosis]] and [[Osteoarthritis]].

General increase in the average price of goods and services in terms of money. Inflation reduces the purchasing power of money and is usually measured as the annualized percentage change in a price index, typically the consumer price index (CPI). Changes are attributed to increases in the money supply, demand shocks, supply shocks such as energy crises, and falls in interest rates set by the central bank. After private banknote currency proliferated during the [[American Civil War]], the term came to refer directly to currency depreciation. Moderate inflation has drawbacks, including uncertainty that may discourage investment and savings, and benefits, such as reducing [[Unemployment|unemployment]] through nominal wage rigidity. Most economists favor a low, steady rate, which central banks pursue mainly by setting interest rates. The opposite of inflation is [[Deflation]].

Academic field concerned with the analysis, collection, classification, storage, retrieval and protection of information. Practitioners study how knowledge is applied and used in organizations, and how people, organizations and information systems interact. The field is transdisciplinary, drawing on [[Computer science]], [[Statistics]], [[Information theory]] and [[Cognitive psychology]], as well as library science and human-computer interaction. It focuses on understanding problems from the perspective of stakeholders before applying information and other technologies. Its objective is to create, replace, improve or understand information systems. Applied areas include health informatics, digital humanities, knowledge management, cybersecurity and information policy. The first known use of the term was in 1955.

Study or use of computers, telecommunication systems and other devices to create, process, store, retrieve and transmit information. The term is commonly used for computers and [[Computer network|computer networks]], but it also covers technologies such as [[Television]] and [[Telephone|telephones]]. An IT system includes all hardware, software and peripheral equipment operated by a limited group of users. The term in its modern sense first appeared in a 1958 *Harvard Business Review* article by Harold J. Leavitt and Thomas L. Whisler. The [[Antikythera mechanism]], dating from about the beginning of the first century BC, is generally considered the earliest known mechanical analog computer. Electronic computers using relays or thermionic valves appeared in the early 1940s, and the Zuse Z3, completed in 1941, was the world's first programmable computer. In the mid-1900s, [[Alan Turing]], J. Presper Eckert and John Mauchly were pioneers of early computer technology.

Mathematical study of the quantification, storage and communication of information. The field was established and formalized by [[Claude Shannon]] in the 1940s, although Harry Nyquist and Ralph Hartley made early contributions in the 1920s. Its key concept is [[Entropy (information theory)|entropy]], which Shannon defined as the lack of information about an event; a fair coin flip carries 1 bit of entropy until its outcome is observed. In *A Mathematical Theory of Communication* (1948), Shannon showed that the achievable rate of reliable communication over a noisy channel approaches the channel capacity. Applications include data compression, as in ZIP files, error correction in DSL, the invention of the [[Compact disc|compact disc]], and the development of the [[Internet]] and artificial intelligence. The theory also reaches into cryptography, linguistics, neurobiology and black holes.

Form of [[Electromagnetic radiation|electromagnetic radiation]] with wavelengths longer than visible light but shorter than [[Microwave|microwaves]]. Infrared begins just beyond red light and is therefore invisible to the human eye. It is generally understood to range from about 780 nm to 30 μm. The astronomer Sir [[William Herschel]] discovered it in 1800 through its effect on a thermometer. Slightly more than half of the energy from the [[Sun]] reaches Earth as infrared, and the balance between absorbed and emitted infrared affects the planet's climate. Humans at normal body temperature radiate chiefly at wavelengths around 10 μm. Uses include night-vision devices, thermal-imaging cameras that detect heat loss and assist firefighting, [[Spectroscopy|spectroscopy]], [[Weather forecasting|weather forecasting]], and military applications such as target acquisition and [[Surveillance|surveillance]].

Swedish filmmaker and theatre director. He is considered one of the greatest and most important filmmakers in the history of cinema. Bergman directed more than 60 films and documentaries, most of which he also wrote, and most of his films were set in Sweden. Many of his films from 1961 onward were filmed on the island of Fårö. His acclaimed works include *The Seventh Seal* (1957), *Wild Strawberries* (1957), *Persona* (1966) and *Fanny and Alexander* (1982), which were included in the 2012 edition of *Sight & Sound's* Greatest Films of All Time. He directed more than 170 plays, including periods as leading director of Sweden's Royal Dramatic Theatre in Stockholm and of Germany's Residenztheater in [[Munich]]. His films earned Academy Award wins and nominations, and he received his personal Irving G. Thalberg Memorial Award. His actors included [[Max von Sydow]].

Swedish actress. Born in [[Stockholm]] to a Swedish father and a German mother, she began her career in Swedish and German films before American audiences knew her from the English-language remake of *Intermezzo* (1939). She starred as Ilsa Lund in *Casablanca* (1942) and won the [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Actress for *Gaslight* (1944). She made three films with [[Alfred Hitchcock]]: *Spellbound* (1945), *Notorious* (1946) and *Under Capricorn* (1949). The revelation of her affair with Roberto Rossellini in 1950 caused a scandal in the United States, and she remained in Europe for several years. She later returned to Hollywood and won two more Academy Awards, for *Anastasia* (1956) and *Murder on the Orient Express* (1974). She also won a Tony Award and two Primetime Emmy Awards, and spoke five languages.

Practice of receiving property, titles, debts, rights and obligations upon the death of an individual. Succession is the legal process by which a deceased person's rights and property pass to heirs, and inheritance is what the heirs receive. Succession occurs either under statutory intestacy rules or according to a valid will, which often must be attested by a notary. [[Common law]] jurisdictions typically require formal probate, while [[Civil law (legal system)|civil law]] systems often let heirs acquire ownership automatically, a principle known as saisine in [[Quebec]]. Historically, patrimonial inheritance passed property only to male descendants, while some societies used matrilineal succession; most modern states use egalitarian inheritance regardless of gender or birth order. A will may disinherit an heir completely, although [[Louisiana]] permits disinheritance only in enumerated circumstances. Inheritance has been compared to nepotism.

Equitable remedy in the form of a court order compelling a party to do or refrain from certain acts. Developed by the English courts of [[Equity (law)|equity]], injunctions trace their origins to the Roman *interdict*. They are generally granted when a wrong cannot be remedied adequately by money damages, and courts also consider the public interest and give special attention to fairness and good faith. An injunction may be prohibitory, forbidding an act such as using an illegally obtained trade secret, or mandatory, requiring action such as cleaning up an oil spill; many combine both. A party that fails to comply faces criminal or civil penalties, including monetary sanctions and possible imprisonment, and may be charged with contempt of court. In [[New South Wales]], Australia, a court may grant an apprehended violence order to a person who fears violence, harassment or stalking.

Gel, sol or solution containing at least one colorant, such as a [[Dye]] or [[Pigment]], used to color a surface to produce an image, text or design. Ink is used for drawing or writing with a pen, brush or quill, and thicker paste inks are used in letterpress and lithographic printing. Modern inks may contain solvents, resins, lubricants and surfactants alongside their colorants. The earliest inks of all civilizations were probably made from lampblack, a [[Soot|soot]] collected as a by-product of fire. Ink was used in ancient Egypt on [[Papyrus]] from at least the 26th century BC, and the earliest Chinese inks may date to four millennia ago. India ink was invented in China. About 1,600 years ago, a popular recipe mixed iron salts with tannin from gallnuts; the ink was bluish-black when first applied and faded to dull brown. Medieval European scribes wrote mainly on [[Parchment]].

Metropolitan region inland from coastal [[Southern California]], centered on Riverside and San Bernardino. Its most comprehensive definition includes all of both counties, an area larger than [[West Virginia]]. The Riverside–San Bernardino–Ontario metropolitan area, as defined by the U.S. Census Bureau, covers more than 27,000 sq mi (70,000 km²) and had a population of about 4.6 million in 2020. At the end of the 19th century, the region was a major center of citrus, dairy and winemaking. Agriculture declined through the 20th century as the population grew, and residential, industrial and commercial development has increased since the 1970s.

Extremely venomous snake of semiarid central-eastern [[Australia]]. First described in 1879, it remained poorly known for nearly 90 years before it was rediscovered in 1972. Based on the median lethal dose of its venom in laboratory mice, it is widely regarded as the most venomous snake in the world. A single bite is estimated to contain enough venom to kill more than 100 adult humans. It preys on [[Mammal|mammals]] and is usually shy and reclusive, rarely encountering people because it lives in remote areas. The word "fierce" in its common names refers to venom strength rather than temperament.

Autonomous region of northern [[China]], whose border includes two-thirds of China's border with [[Mongolia]]. Officially the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, it was established in 1947 and is China's third-largest administrative subdivision, covering about 1,200,000 km² (12% of China's total land area). Its capital is Hohhot, and other major cities include Baotou, Chifeng, Tongliao and Ordos. It recorded a population of 24,706,321 in the 2010 census. [[Han Chinese]] make up the majority, while [[Mongols]] number over 4 million, the largest Mongol population in the world. Annual GDP per capita was US$14,343 (2022), ranked 8th in China. Before the rise of the Mongols in the 13th century, the Hetao region alternated in control between Chinese farming communities and nomadic peoples such as the [[Xiongnu]].

Vector space equipped with an inner product, a generalization of the [[Dot product|dot product]]. The inner product defines lengths, angles and orthogonality, and it induces a norm, so every inner product space is a normed vector space. If the space is also complete, it is a [[Hilbert space]]. Spaces over the complex numbers are sometimes called unitary spaces. Infinite-dimensional inner product spaces are widely used in [[Functional analysis]]. The concept was first used by Giuseppe Peano in 1898.

Chemical compound that lacks carbon–hydrogen bonds. The study of inorganic compounds is a subfield known as [[Inorganic chemistry]]. Inorganic compounds comprise most of the [[Earth's crust|Earth's crust]], and all allotropes of carbon, such as graphite and diamond, are often considered inorganic. Simple carbon compounds such as [[Carbon dioxide]], carbon monoxide, carbonates and cyanides are also often considered inorganic. Many of these compounds occur normally within organisms, and describing a chemical as inorganic does not mean it cannot occur in living things. In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler converted ammonium cyanate into [[Urea]], an event often cited as the starting point of modern organic chemistry. IUPAC does not offer a definition of the term.

Catholic judicial procedure, and the tribunals that used it, to combat heresy and related offenses. The name came to denote medieval and Reformation-era state-organized tribunals targeting heresy, apostasy, blasphemy, [[Witchcraft]] and customs considered deviant. Inquisitions began in 12th-century France against the Cathars and Waldensians. From the 1250s, inquisitors were generally chosen from the Dominican Order rather than local clergy. The [[Spanish Inquisition|Spanish]] and Portuguese inquisitions often focused on conversos, former [[Jews|Jews]] who had converted to Christianity, and moriscos, [[Muslims|Muslims]] who had been forced to convert. Inquisitions used violence, isolation and torture, or the threat of torture, to extract confessions. After the [[Reformation]], the [[Counter-Reformation]] expanded the inquisitions. Apart from the [[Papal States]], inquisition courts were abolished in the early 19th century.

[[Sleep disorder]] causing difficulty falling asleep or staying asleep for as long as desired. It is typically followed by daytime sleepiness, low energy, irritability and depressed mood. Chronic insomnia involves at least three episodes per week for at least three months. It can result from [[Pain|chronic pain]], [[Heart failure]], psychological stress, or the use of [[Caffeine]], [[Nicotine]] and alcohol. Cognitive behavioral therapy is considered the first-line treatment, and sleeping pills are usually not recommended for more than four or five weeks. Between 10% and 30% of adults have insomnia at any given point in time. Women and people over 65 are affected more often.

Photo and short-form video sharing social networking service owned by Meta Platforms. Development began in [[San Francisco]] as Burbn, a check-in app, before it was refocused on photo sharing and renamed Instagram, a blend of "instant camera" and "telegram." It launched for iOS in October 2010, and [[Facebook]] acquired it in April 2012 for approximately US$1 billion in cash and stock. Early posts were limited to a square format, a restriction raised to 1080 pixels in 2015. As of January 2019, Stories was used by 500 million people daily. The service supports 33 languages.

Inherent inclination of a living organism toward a particular complex behavior, containing innate elements. Any behavior performed without prior experience is instinctive, and every animal has instincts, including humans. Examples include newly hatched [[Sea turtle|sea turtles]] moving toward the ocean, a [[Marsupial]] climbing into its mother's pouch at birth, animal courtship, and nest building. The simplest instinctive behavior is a fixed action pattern, a short sequence of actions carried out without variation in response to a clearly defined stimulus. Instincts differ from [[Reflex|reflexes]], which are simple responses to a specific stimulus. Although their innate characteristics are invariant, experience can change the details of their performance. Jean Henri Fabre regarded instincts as fixed patterns that do not change in novel situations.

Humanly devised structure of rules and norms that shape and constrain social behavior. All definitions entail a level of persistence and continuity, and institutions range from formal laws and rules to informal social conventions. Primary or meta-institutions, such as the [[Family]] or [[Money]], are broad enough to encompass sets of related institutions. Institutions are a principal object of study in [[Political science]], [[Anthropology]], economics and [[Sociology]], which [[Émile Durkheim]] described as the "science of institutions, their genesis and their functioning." Definitions vary in formality: broad ones include informal practices such as handshakes, while narrow ones require formal laws and complex organizational structures. Institutions have been described as the social science equivalent of theories in the natural sciences.

Collective term for measuring instruments used to indicate, measure and record physical quantities. It is also the field of making such instruments, which involves [[Metrology]], [[Automation]] and [[Control theory]]. Instruments range from simple direct-reading [[Thermometer|thermometers]] to multi-sensor components of industrial control systems, and are found in laboratories, refineries, factories, vehicles and homes. They measure parameters including pressure, flow, temperature, humidity, density, viscosity, frequency, voltage and position. Pneumatic transmitters and automatic 3-term (PID) controllers were introduced in the early 1930s, with a signal of 3 to 15 psi as the typical standard. Transistor electronics later allowed wiring to replace pipes, and the 4–20 mA signal was eventually standardized as ANSI/ISA S50.

Peptide hormone produced by beta cells of the [[Pancreas|pancreatic]] islets. It is the main anabolic hormone of the body, regulating the metabolism of carbohydrates, fats and protein. It promotes the absorption of [[Glucose]] from the blood into the liver, fat and skeletal muscle, where glucose is converted into glycogen or fat, and it lowers blood sugar. Glucagon from neighboring alpha cells opposes it. Decreased or absent insulin activity causes [[Diabetes]]. In type 1 diabetes, beta cells are destroyed by an autoimmune reaction, while type 2 diabetes involves reduced beta-cell function and insulin resistance in peripheral tissues. Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin from dog pancreas at the [[University of Toronto]] in 1921. [[Frederick Sanger]] sequenced it in 1951, making insulin the first protein to be fully sequenced.

Violent armed rebellion by small, lightly armed bands practicing guerrilla warfare against a larger authority. The conflict is asymmetric: insurgents avoid large-scale direct battles and blend into the civilian population, often in [[Rural area|rural areas]], to gradually expand territorial control. Because of this blending, insurgencies tend to involve considerable violence against civilians by both the state and the insurgents. An insurgency aims for political control rather than indiscriminate violence, which distinguishes it from [[Terrorism]], although it may incorporate terrorist tactics. Insurgencies can be multipolar: during the [[Angolan Civil War]] the main sides were the MPLA and UNITA, while the separatist FLEC movement sought independence for Cabinda. The Confederate States of America was not recognized as a sovereign state during the [[American Civil War]], but it was recognized as a belligerent power, so its revolt may not be viewed as an insurgency.

Continuous analog of a sum, used to calculate areas, volumes and their generalizations. Integration, the process of computing an integral, is one of the two fundamental operations of calculus, along with [[Derivative|differentiation]]. A definite integral computes the signed area of the region bounded by a function's graph between two points, while an indefinite integral is an antiderivative. The [[Fundamental theorem of calculus|fundamental theorem of calculus]] relates the two operations and allows a definite integral to be computed from a known antiderivative. Integration was initially used to find areas under curves and displacement from velocity. [[Isaac Newton]] and [[Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz]] formulated its principles independently in the late 17th century, and [[Bernhard Riemann]] later gave a rigorous definition. Henri Lebesgue generalized it in the early 20th century.
